 COP31 must deliver climate justice for displaced people
 Published : 26 October 2026
 • 
 Updated : 26 October 2026, 12:58
 • 
 VIEWS
 SHARE 
 Farah Kabir
 Farah Kabir 
 Displacement means losing more than just a home; it can cost families their livelihoods, access to essential services, and community ties. FILE PHOTO: HABIBUR RAHMAN 
 By 2050, Bangladesh could see 1.33 crore of its population becoming internal climate migrants, according to the Asian Development Bank’s Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026. The report links this risk to rising seas, water scarcity, and declining agricultural productivity. Who pays when people lose homes, land and livelihoods to a crisis they did little to create? 
 Disasters already displaced people within Bangladesh 1.47 crore times between 2014 and 2023. These are displacement movements, not distinct individuals. Separately, an assessment by the International Organization for Migration, together with the Bangladesh government, estimated that nearly 50 lakh people were internally displaced by disasters when data were collected from September and October in 2025. Nearly 63 percent were displaced before April 2020. The last figure covers disaster-induced displacement, not climate-attributable displacement alone.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 Displacement strips away far more than a home. Families can lose land, income, savings, education, healthcare, and the social networks that sustain them. Women lose the few assets they may have, as well as compensation rights, while shouldering more unpaid care. Persons with disabilities, older people and marginalised communities face further barriers when assistance and infrastructure are inaccessible. Communities are not passive victims. They diversify livelihoods, draw on family networks, borrow money, sell assets, move temporarily for work, or migrate when staying becomes untenable. These strategies show ingenuity, but also the limits of adaptation when households exhaust savings, take on debt, or leave home to survive. 
 Mobility can be part of adaptation when people have information, resources, rights, and genuine choices. Without safe shelter or viable livelihoods, distress-driven displacement deepens impoverishment. Policy must support people before, during and after movement.
 Bangladesh has established foundations for action. Its National Strategy on Internal Displacement Management, 2021 and National Action Plan (2022-2042) provide a framework for durable solutions. The National Adaptation Plan (2023-2050) and Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 offer further instruments. The National Framework and Action Plan for Locally Led Adaptation , launched in February 2026, offers an opportunity to connect community priorities with public investment. It is critical to integrate development plans with climate action. The test is whether commitments reach people where they live and those already forced to move. That requires a shift in how adaptation is financed. 
 Funding must support community-led risk reduction, resilient housing, freshwater, livelihood diversification, early warning, and social protection. It must also recognise mobility as a legitimate adaptation response where staying is no longer safe or viable. Local organisations and displaced people need accessible, predictable funding and real influence over decisions.
 The adaptation fund and other mechanisms must turn locally led adaptation commitments into support for displaced and displacement-prone communities. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has a different, complementary role: addressing harms that cannot be prevented through mitigation and adaptation alone. Its resources must help people recover from destroyed homes, lost land and livelihoods, disrupted communities, and cultural losses. Neither form of finance should be reduced to emergency relief after disaster strikes.
 Durable solutions require more. Destination towns need affordable housing, decent work, transport, healthcare, education, and social protection. National policies must anticipate movement, preparing likely destination towns and cities with climate-resilient infrastructure and essential services, alongside social protection systems that can reach newly displaced people and host communities. 
 At COP31, leaders must confront the gap between climate promises and people already adapting, moving and rebuilding. Major emitters who continue to emit must cut emissions faster and honour climate finance obligations. Finance must be adequate, accessible and grant-based, without adding to the debt burdens constraining public investment. 
 Bangladesh must implement its plans and prepare towns and cities receiving displaced people. But disasters don’t strike a level playing field: they deepen existing inequalities, push already disadvantaged households further into poverty, and make recovery harder with every successive shock. That’s precisely why the country cannot be left to finance a global crisis alone. Those who contributed least to climate change must not be left to bear its greatest human costs—first through the loss of home and livelihood, then through systems that fail to protect their rights and support recovery.
 Farah Kabir is country director at ActionAid Bangladesh.
